findings.title: Session type is wrong for the first access token issued with offline_access
findings.body:
The session type is taken from `userSession.isOffline()`. In the code-to-token and password grants with `scope=offline_access`, the access token is created from the online user session before `generateRefreshToken()` creates the offline session.

As a result, that access token is encoded as `on` (online). Right afterwards the online session is removed: always in `ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`, and when `FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS` is set in `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`. The token then advertises an online session that no longer exists; the session survives only as offline.

The stated purpose is to look up only the encoded session type (#37662). Any such consumer would fail to find the session and reject a valid token. Use `clientSessionContext.isOfflineTokenRequested()` (or equivalent) to decide between offline and online.

findings.title: Grant type only recorded for grants that go through createTokenResponse; client_credentials (and UMA) end up as 'na'
findings.body:
`Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is set on the client session context only in `createTokenResponse`, plus explicitly in ROPC, pre-authorized code, refresh and standard token exchange.

`ClientCredentialsGrantType` builds its response via `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` without calling `createTokenResponse`, and this PR does not change it. The permission (UMA) grant also does not use `createTokenResponse`.

Tokens from these grants are therefore encoded with the unknown grant `na`, even though shortcuts `cc` and `pg` were added to their factories. This silently defeats the feature for the client-credentials case. No test catches it, because `expectClientLogin` does not check `TOKEN_ID`.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher never verifies the grant type (inverted condition and wrong offset)
findings.body:
The encoded prefix is 2 chars of session type, 2 of token type and 2 of grant type, so the grant is at indices 4-6. The matcher reads `substring(3, 5)` instead (e.g. `"ta"` for `onrtac`), which can never equal a grant shortcut.

On top of that, the condition is inverted: it returns `false` when the shortcut *matches*. The net effect is that the matcher accepts any grant type as long as the suffix is a UUID.

All updated `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` assertions are therefore vacuous with respect to grant type. The check should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` plus a length check on `items[0]`.

findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant type factories at startup
findings.body:
`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` without a default implementation.

Any custom `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` compiled against the previous SPI will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()`, which prevents server startup. A custom implementation returning `null` would instead cause an NPE from `ConcurrentHashMap.put`.

Consider a default implementation (or a fallback to `na`) and handling of null shortcuts instead of failing boot.

findings.title: Javadoc recommends 3-letter shortcuts, but encoding/decoding requires exactly 2 characters with no validation
findings.body:
The Javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters". However, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` hard-codes a 6-character prefix and takes characters 4-6 as the grant shortcut.

A custom grant that follows the doc and returns a 3-letter shortcut will produce token ids (e.g. `onrtabc:...`) that the same provider cannot decode; it throws "Expected length of 6".

Neither `postInit` nor the lazy refresh paths in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` validate shortcut length. The doc should say exactly 2 characters, and the factory should reject other lengths.

findings.title: Copy-paste: null check for rawTokenId validates grantType instead
findings.body:
The line meant to enforce non-null `rawTokenId` is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`. It re-checks `grantType`, so a null `rawTokenId` is accepted silently.

`encodeTokenId` would then produce an id ending in `:null`. It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

findings.title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of an NPE, not the intended validation
findings.body:
In this test the factory's `sessionFactory` is null. For the unknown shortcut `ac`, `getGrantTypeByShortcut` falls into the refresh branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws `NullPointerException`.

The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes without ever reaching the `IllegalArgumentException("... Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` path. It should assert on `IllegalArgumentException` and set up a (mock) session factory.

findings.title: Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from SPI class
findings.body:
The public `OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context)` copy constructor is deleted rather than updated to copy the new `grantType` field.

Custom grant implementations or wrappers that used it to derive or modify a context will fail to compile or link. This removal is unrelated to the feature, which only needed the new field copied. Keep the constructor and copy `grantType` in it.

findings.title: Lazy map refresh can silently overwrite existing shortcut mappings
findings.body:
`postInit` detects duplicate shortcuts by comparing map sizes. The lazy refresh in `getShortcutByGrantType` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut` instead blindly `put`s into both maps.

A newly deployed grant whose shortcut collides with an existing one would overwrite the mapping in `grantsByShortcuts`. Previously issued tokens would then decode to the wrong grant type, and the two maps would become inconsistent. The two maps are also updated non-atomically.

The refresh paths should apply the same collision and length validation, e.g. via `putIfAbsent` and rejecting conflicts.

findings.title: Access token jti is no longer a UUID
findings.body:
The access token `jti` changes from a 36-char UUID to a prefixed form, e.g. `onrtac:<uuid>`, 43 chars containing `:`.

Resource servers or integrations that parse or validate `jti` as a UUID, or store it in fixed-length/UUID-typed columns for replay detection, will break after upgrade. This externally visible format change is not documented in upgrade/migration notes in this PR.
